subject: Accounting
title: Ghost Employees and Phantom Vendors
description: A short lesson to help you apply Ghost Employees and Phantom Vendors.

hook.text: A payroll clerk adds a fake employee. Every two weeks, a check is issued—and the clerk cashes it.

buildup.text: Ghost employees are fictitious workers on the payroll. Phantom vendors are fake companies billing for nothing.

discovery.text: Both schemes funnel real money to fake entities—controlled by the fraudster.

twist.text: These frauds can last years. One case found 30 ghost employees earning $2.5 million combined.

climax.text: Cross-referencing employee addresses, bank accounts, and tax IDs reveals duplicates and fakes.

punchline.text: If the employee doesn't exist, the paycheck shouldn't either.

quiz.question: How can ghost employee fraud be detected?
options: Cross-referencing addresses, bank accounts, and tax IDs

details.summary: Ghost employee and phantom vendor schemes create fictitious people or companies in payroll and purchasing systems to siphon money. This topic explains how these schemes work, the internal controls that prevent them, and the red flags that reveal them.
details.whyItMatters: Ghost and phantom schemes are among the most costly occupational frauds because they can be automated to run indefinitely. A single fraudster can extract millions before detection.
takeaways: Ghost employees are fictitious payroll entries whose payments are diverted to the fraudster
Phantom vendors submit invoices for goods or services that were never delivered
Segregation of duties—separating who creates, approves, and pays—is the primary prevention control

faq.question: How do ghost employee schemes work?
faq.answer: A person with payroll access creates a fictitious employee record and directs the paychecks to a bank account they control. The ghost employee has no work product, no badge access, and often a missing or fabricated address—all detectable through proper controls.

faq.question: How can organizations detect phantom vendor schemes?
faq.answer: Red flags include vendors with P.O. box-only addresses, vendors with no phone number or website, vendor addresses or bank accounts matching those of employees, invoices with no purchase order reference, and vendors that only bill for services (harder to verify delivery than physical goods).
